newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin starts with high popularity - polls.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin starts with high popularity - polls.

text.p: France's new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin is enjoying a honeymoon with voters, judging by the first wave of opinion polls conducted since he took office last week.

However, the polls published on Thursday showed opinion divided on President Jacques Chirac since the snap parliamentary election he called backfired on him. Two showed his approval rating falling since the defeat of his centre-right allies in the June 1 vote while the third showing his popularity on the mend.

A Sofres poll for the weekly Le Figaro magazine found that 63 percent had confidence in Jospin's ability to solve France's problems, 32 percent lacked confidence in him and five percent had no opinion.
An Ipsos survey for the weekly Le Point said 44 percent had a favourable opinion of Jospin, 21 percent an unfavourable view and 35 percent no opinion.

A Louis Harris survey for the weekly Valeurs Actuelles showed 43 percent of people had a good first impression of Jospin's actions as prime minister, against 15 percent with a poor view. But 42 percent declined to give an opinion.
Jospin came to office unexpectedly after Chirac's disastrous gamble on the snap election, intended to give his centre-right allies another five years in government.
The Sofres poll said that 41 percent had confidence in Chirac, an increase of three points since a similar poll conducted a month earlier.
But the Louis Harris poll indicated that just 32 percent of French people had a good impression of Chirac's actions as president, down from 37 percent last month.
And the Ipsos survey found that just 35 percent had a favourable view of Chirac, down from 46 percent.
Chirac's rating in the Harris survey was the lowest since a 29-64 percent split in November 1996, the polling firm said.

The Harris survey also showed that 42 percent of people reckoned the economic and social climate in France was getting worse, down from 52 percent a month ago. But just nine percent thought things were improving, down from 10 percent in May.
Those believing the situation was unchanged rose to 45 percent from 37.
The Louis Harris survey, of 1,004 people, was carried out on June 6-7, as was the Ipsos poll, which questioned 940 individuals. The Sofres poll of 1,000 individuals was conducted on June 4-6.
